title: When Teachers Answer Their Own Questions
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Dan Meyer examines math teacher questions that give away their own answers, such as 'Aren't all these slopes positive?' and 'Are you sure about that?', drawn from the 1999 TIMSS classroom videos. He argues that such questions waste time because students can answer them from the teacher's intonation alone, so neither the student's thinking nor the teacher's information improves, though everyone feels successful. He relays coach Jenna Laib's alternatives: use a stock question like 'How do you know?' regardless of correctness, adopt an interpretive or generative listening stance rather than an evaluative one, and open the answer space with questions like 'Which of these slopes are positive?'. The rest of the post is a conference tour list and an odds-and-ends section on student AI protests, Google's AI overviews, ProPublica's easy private school, and a piece on explanation and learning.
points: Leading questions invite students to read the teacher's tone instead of thinking about the math, and they hide what students actually understand.
They feel good because the student enjoys an illusion of understanding and the teacher enjoys an illusion of order, which is why they persist.
A stock follow-up question asked regardless of accuracy removes the tonal hint, though students will protest the loss of their cue at first.
Teachers can also check their listening stance, evaluative versus interpretive versus generative, since only evaluating gives the game away.
Reframing a yes-or-no leading question into an open one, such as 'Which of these slopes are positive?', opens the answer space.
quotes: Putting it bluntly: these questions are a waste of breath and time. Math teacher questions, at minimum, should help students think more about math.

These questions, instead, invite students to think about the teacher’s intonation. They don’t give the teacher any information about how the student understands math because you don’t need to understand math to answer them.
The kid enjoys the illusion of understanding. The teacher enjoys the illusion of a well-ordered class. But effective math teachers understand this is only an illusion.

One thing that helps is having a stock question to repeat over and over again. How do you know? How did you decide? If teachers ask the same question regardless of accuracy of the student’s answer, the students recognize that the words aren’t a hint.
It’s important for teachers to persist through the early stage of using a stock question, because students will be annoyed that they lost their vocal cue.
If we only ever listen with an evaluative stance, the follow-up questions and intonations give us away.
After 37 years in the classroom, the distinction between “Does this technology work?” and “What does it actually do to the experience of learning?” feels crucial to me.
